claims.claim: Harrison (in comments) states Under Heaven's sections with women viewpoint characters are in present tense while male-viewpoint sections are in past tense.
Harrison quotes the narrator's remark that only a patient historian or a story-shaper would note such conjunctions, as Kay's self-reflexive use of history.
claims.quote: Only a patient historian with access to records

claims.claim: Walton names Kay's Sarantine style an odd, distanced, elegiac 'veiled omniscient': a narrator who knows everything but draws and lifts veils.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Mosaics and charioteers: Guy Gavriel Kay's Sarantine Mosaic', Tor.com/Reactor (2009-11-02)
claims.quote: odd, distanced, elegaic style that I want to call veiled omniscient

claims.claim: Walton dislikes Kay's Dunnett-like trick of describing a character for pages without saying who is who.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Mosaics and charioteers: Guy Gavriel Kay's Sarantine Mosaic', Tor.com/Reactor (2009-11-02)
claims.quote: plays tricks where he described but doesn’t say who is who

claims.claim: Walton says there is always a pulling back, events interpreted through a consciousness of artifice, like the wrong end of a telescope.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Mosaics and charioteers: Guy Gavriel Kay's Sarantine Mosaic', Tor.com/Reactor (2009-11-02)

claims.claim: Walton notes many points of view but Kay never takes up a character just to throw them away; ironic omniscient linking underlines everything.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Mosaics and charioteers: Guy Gavriel Kay's Sarantine Mosaic', Tor.com/Reactor (2009-11-02)
claims.quote: he never takes up a character just to throw them away

claims.claim: Walton observes the books concentrate on single days with heavy flashback, using more pluperfect than anything she can think of, almost like Ulysses.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Mosaics and charioteers: Guy Gavriel Kay's Sarantine Mosaic', Tor.com/Reactor (2009-11-02)
claims.quote: more use of the pluperfect tense in these than anything else

claims.claim: Walton notes a chariot race is seen from a driver, someone in the crowd and an undercook making soup.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Mosaics and charioteers: Guy Gavriel Kay's Sarantine Mosaic', Tor.com/Reactor (2009-11-02)
claims.quote: an undercook for the Blue faction making soup

claims.claim: Walton says Kay mediates the world through chariot races and mosaic-making, describing heresy and empire in those terms.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Mosaics and charioteers: Guy Gavriel Kay's Sarantine Mosaic', Tor.com/Reactor (2009-11-02)
claims.quote: mediates the world through the chariot races

claims.claim: Walton praises details real enough to bite: tesserae quality, mud, fish sauces, the arrow-extraction tool.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Mosaics and charioteers: Guy Gavriel Kay's Sarantine Mosaic', Tor.com/Reactor (2009-11-02)
claims.quote: The details are all real enough to bite

claims.claim: Walton argues renaming reshuffles the deck so no reader knows the ending: a historical novel is inevitably tragedy, a historical fantasy is open.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Mosaics and charioteers: Guy Gavriel Kay's Sarantine Mosaic', Tor.com/Reactor (2009-11-02)

claims.claim: Walton says the little magic runs glinting through everything like silver threads in shot silk.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Mosaics and charioteers: Guy Gavriel Kay's Sarantine Mosaic', Tor.com/Reactor (2009-11-02)
claims.quote: like the silver threads in shot silk

claims.claim: Walton finds Arbonne mannered, distanced and held at arm's length, its world denser than its gossamer characters.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Provencal Fantasy: Guy Gavriel Kay's A Song for Arbonne', Tor.com/Reactor (2010-08-06)
claims.quote: mannered and distanced and held at arm’s length

claims.claim: Walton remembers Arbonne chiefly through set-piece moments of the kind Kay does so well.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Provencal Fantasy: Guy Gavriel Kay's A Song for Arbonne', Tor.com/Reactor (2010-08-06)
claims.quote: a few set-piece moments, of the kind Kay does so well

claims.claim: Walton traces a trajectory away from magic from Fionavar through Tigana and Arbonne to Lions.
claims.source: Jo Walton, 'Provencal Fantasy: Guy Gavriel Kay's A Song for Arbonne', Tor.com/Reactor (2010-08-06)

verdicts.trueWording: the sections with women viewpoint characters ... are in present tense, compared to sections with male viewpoint characters in past tense
verdicts.note: Niall's own comment (Aug 19 2010, 7:34 am) on his Vector review; quote 'are in present tense' exact. Live URL 403s behind a JS proof-of-work wall; raw page read via Wayback id_ capture 20250916021402.

verdicts.trueWording: “Only a patient historian with access to records is likely to discover such links,” Kay writes; only “someone shaping a story for palace or marketplace … would note these conjunctions”
verdicts.note: Both halves quoted verbatim by Harrison and framed as 'The novelistic attention to coincidence becomes an illustration' of story-making from history, alongside 'As the implied narrator becomes a real narrator'. Harrison attributes with 'Kay writes' rather than 'the narrator', but the quoted words are the novel's narration (p.542). Wayback raw capture.

verdicts.trueWording: written in an odd, distanced, elegaic style that I want to call veiled omniscient
verdicts.note: Page continues: 'The omniscient narrator knows what will happen ... He draws and lifts veils.' Note Walton spells it 'elegaic'.

verdicts.trueWording: He plays tricks where he described but doesn’t say who is who—does anybody like this? I hate it when Dorothy Dunnett does it
verdicts.note: Dunnett named explicitly; 'don’t leave me guessing who it is for two pages' supports the for-pages limb.
Same paragraph: 'interpreted through the consciousness of artifice' and 'always looking through the wrong end of the telescope'.

verdicts.trueWording: There are many points of view, but he never takes up a character just to throw them away
verdicts.note: Next sentence: 'The ironic linking of everything together in omniscient connects and underlines'.

verdicts.trueWording: there’s more use of the pluperfect tense in these than anything else I can think of
verdicts.note: Same paragraph: 'concentrate on single days ... with lots of flashbacks' and 'This single day thing is almost like Ulysses'.

verdicts.trueWording: see it from the point of view of a driver, someone in the crowd, an undercook for the Blue faction making soup
verdicts.note: All three strata named in one sentence about a chariot race.

verdicts.trueWording: Kay mediates the world through the chariot races and the making of mosaics
verdicts.note: Followed by 'We get the heresy and the religion through the mosaics. We get life and control of the empire through the chariot racing.'

verdicts.trueWording: The details are all real enough to bite, the varying quality of the glass tesserae, the mud, the fish sauces, the tool for drawing out arrows from flesh
verdicts.note: All four listed details present verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: a historical novel is inevitably a tragedy, a historical fantasy is open
verdicts.note: Reshuffle limb: 'because you have changed the names and reshuffled the deck, nobody knows what’s going to happen'.

verdicts.trueWording: It’s not much magic, but it runs glinting through everything else like the silver threads in shot silk
verdicts.note: Preceded by the inventory of the small magic (soul-birds, one god encounter, flashes of flame, prophetic dreams).

verdicts.trueWording: it’s all mannered and distanced and held at arm’s length
verdicts.note: Gossamer limb: 'the world is more memorable and somehow denser than the characters, who are in comparison gossamer.'

verdicts.trueWording: The characters, however, and the plot, had vanished from my mind ... except for a few set-piece moments
verdicts.note: Quote is exact, but Walton's 'except' applies to characters and plot only — the same sentence-pair says 'I remembered the setting perfectly well' (lavender fields, Court of Love, troubadours), so set-pieces are not how she chiefly remembers the book.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that she remembers Arbonne chiefly through set-pieces — she remembered the setting perfectly well; only characters and plot had vanished

verdicts.trueWording: This is also a trajectory away from magic—Fionavar is full of magic, Tigana has somewhat less, Arbonne has less again, and The Lions of Al-Rassan has nothing but an accurate prophecy
verdicts.note: All four books named in the stated order.
